rounds.response:
By [Minister’s Name]

We face two urgent tasks at once: to keep household costs under control today, and to protect the jobs and living standards that underpin tomorrow’s economy. That is why my government is putting a predictable, economy‑wide carbon price at the centre of a broader plan to cut emissions affordably, shield ordinary families, and give business the certainty it needs to invest here at home.

Let me be clear about what this package is for. A well‑designed carbon price is the most cost‑effective lever we have to reduce emissions at scale: it gives households and firms a clear signal to use less fossil fuel and choose cleaner alternatives, and it channels private investment into the low‑carbon industries that will be the foundation of future jobs. But it is not an abstract exercise in economics. The revenues from this policy are being recycled back to protect ordinary families and to support communities and sectors facing the biggest transitions.

We designed the package with fairness front of mind. Targeted rebates and explicit cost‑of‑living offsets are calibrated to shield most low‑ and middle‑income households on average if we implement the parameters set out in our plan. In practical terms, that means direct payments to households that substantially offset any modest price increases for everyday goods like fuel and home energy, combined with accelerated energy‑efficiency programs and retrofit grants that actively reduce household bills over time. While no policy eliminates every single cost pressure, most ordinary families will be protected on average—and many will be better off once the savings from insulation, heat pumps, and more efficient appliances are taken into account.

To make this concrete, consider a typical working family: two parents, two school‑age children, one car, and a mortgage. Under our plan they will receive direct, timely rebates designed to neutralize near‑term cost effects; they will also be eligible for subsidised home‑efficiency upgrades that cut heating and cooling bills and reduce the need for petrol and diesel. Taken together, these measures are aimed to offset or exceed the modest increases a higher‑consuming household might otherwise see, and to lock in long‑term savings that ease cost‑of‑living pressures rather than worsen them.

We must also be honest about the narrow reality opponents like to highlight: a small number of higher‑consuming households may face modest net costs. That is deliberate and fair—those who use more carbon‑intensive energy will pay proportionately, while the revenue raised helps protect families who are least able to shoulder additional costs. It is also manageable: the rebate parameters, efficiency programs, and targeted supports are designed so that hardship is avoided and the benefits are widely felt.

Business and competitiveness were addressed from the start. Our carbon price is phased in to give firms time to adjust; genuinely trade‑exposed industries receive calibrated protections and transition support; and we are developing a border carbon approach to ensure domestic firms aren’t undercut by lower‑carbon standards abroad. Predictability is as important as the price level—investors make long‑term decisions on the basis of clear rules, and backing away now would only increase uncertainty, delay investment in clean supply chains, and raise the eventual cost of decarbonisation.

Finally, this is about jobs in every region. The transition is already creating work in home retrofits, renewable energy construction, grid upgrades, and clean manufacturing. That’s why we are pairing the carbon price with a dedicated regional investment and retraining fund, local procurement for clean projects, and supports for firms to convert their capabilities to low‑carbon production. The result is a practical pathway for towns and regions to capture new opportunities: from insulation businesses winning local retrofit contracts to manufacturing firms retraining staff for heat‑pump assembly or battery components.

The political choice in front of us is not between cost‑of‑living support and climate action; it is about choosing a fair, credible approach that does both. If we back away now, we risk losing credibility, stalling investment, and making future emissions reductions harder and more expensive—outcomes that would hurt households and workers most. By contrast, staying the course allows us to deliver predictable, cost‑effective emissions reductions while using the proceeds to protect families and create new local jobs.

That is the balance this package strikes: cost‑effective climate action, designed fairness for ordinary families, and predictable signals for business. It is a pragmatic plan that tackles both the immediate pressures people feel in their wallets and the longer‑term economic transition our country must make. We will stand by it, implement it carefully, and make sure the benefits are felt in neighbourhoods and workplaces across the country.
